analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to pass a law before any federal regulation can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing: introduced May 17, 2001 with 7 cosponsors, referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, and it died there with no further action when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would forbid any federal regulation from taking effect until both houses of Congress and the president passed a bill containing the regulation's exact text. Agencies would still write rules, but each one would need an affirmative act of Congress, with fast-tracked floor procedures: no committee review, one hour of debate, no amendments, and a required vote within 60 days. Supporters pitched this as restoring accountability for laws written by unelected officials; the practical effect is that most of the thousands of rules agencies issue each year — safety, health, environmental, and financial standards — could never be issued.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that face federal regulation would gain the most: a requirement that Congress affirmatively pass every rule would effectively shut down most rulemaking, sparing regulated firms compliance costs and blocking new standards before they start. Supporters also argue voters would gain, because the elected officials who actually answer to them would have to put their names on every rule.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries and their lobbying arms

how_it_helps.text: No regulation could take effect before Congress enacted a bill made up solely of that regulation's text, making elected lawmakers directly responsible for every federal rule.
The stated purpose was to end the practice of Congress delegating lawmaking to unaccountable executive-branch officials and to protect the public from rules elected officials will not own.

Bills to enact regulations would get expedited treatment — no committee referral, one hour of debate, no amendments, and a guaranteed floor vote within 60 days — so individual rules could not be quietly buried.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal rules would bear the cost: Congress passes on the order of a couple hundred laws per term while agencies issue thousands of rules, so requiring a separate act of Congress for each rule would leave air, water, workplace, drug, food, and financial standards unwritten or expired. Agencies would also lose their ability to translate broadly written statutes into enforceable standards.

drawbacks.text: The mechanism would bring most federal rulemaking to a halt: agencies issue far more rules each year than Congress could consider, so essential standards — including those implementing food safety, workplace safety, and environmental laws — could not be issued or updated.

The expedited procedures cut Congress's own deliberation short: regulatory bills skip committee entirely, face a one-hour debate cap, and cannot be amended, so members would vote on lengthy technical texts without review.

Supporters would respond that the current system is the real problem: unelected agency staff write rules that carry the force of law, and voters have no way to hold them accountable at the ballot box.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument has real substance — a rule with the force of law ought to trace to someone voters can remove. But the mechanism is a near-shutdown of regulation, not a refinement of it. Weighing them, the costs would fall on the public protections that agency rules deliver, while the savings would flow to the firms those rules constrain. A narrower version — requiring votes on major or costly rules, as later congressional review bills did — would have preserved most of the accountability argument at far less risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sam Brownback introduced the Congressional Responsibility Act of 2001 on May 17, 2001, with 7 Republican cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs the same day; that was the last action of any kind in the record.
The bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Anyone who relies on federal regulation is better off that the bill died: agencies kept their authority to issue binding health, safety, environmental, and financial rules without needing an act of Congress for each one. The industries the bill would have shielded from new rules gained nothing, though they also lost nothing beyond the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyone who relies on federal regulation

for.name: Sam Brownback
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on May 17, 2001.

against.name: Joe Lieberman
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: As committee chair after Democrats took Senate control in June 2001, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill had no actions after referral.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 7 cosponsors were Republicans — 7 of the Senate's 49 — and no Democrat supported it; no hearing or vote ever occurred, so no roll call exists.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturers, energy producers, financial firms)
industries.note: Requiring Congress to affirmatively enact every regulation would have stopped most new rules, sparing these firms compliance costs and blocking future standards before they were written. The public would bear the loss of the protections those rules provide.
Agencies would keep drafting rules but lose the power to give them force of law, reducing them to advisory bodies. Their loss tracks directly with the public's loss of enforceable standards.
These groups depend on agency rulemaking to convert broadly written statutes into specific, enforceable protections. A rule-by-Congress system would leave most of that work undone.
